lead: Don't just look at what it costs to buy. Look at what you'll pay later and what you'll get back.
when: When you're buying equipment, subscribing to a service, choosing how to get around, or deciding whether an upgrade is worth it, this comes up easily.
body:
A cheap printer may come with expensive ink cartridges, and an automation tool still takes time to set up after you buy it. Cost-benefit analysis means laying out and comparing the main things you give and get over a period of time. Costs aren't just money. They include learning, upkeep, the space something takes up, and the other things you can't do because of it.

Cost-benefit analysis systematically compares the relevant costs and expected benefits of an action against a clear baseline for comparison and within a defined time frame. When outcomes can be measured in money and spread over time, the time value of money usually needs to be considered too.

"Benefits" can't always be turned into money either. Ease, convenience, and time with family are worth considering too. Work out the parts you can calculate, and list the hard-to-price parts separately. There's no need to slap a dollar amount on every kind of happiness just to look scientific.
example:
You want to buy a dishwasher, and the price makes you think it's too expensive. But if you only compare the purchase price, you miss installation, supplies, and space, and you also miss the washing-up time you'd save every day. First estimate how often your household cooks, whether your dishes are a good fit, and who'll load and maintain it, then compare that with keeping on washing by hand.

In the end it might be worth buying, or it might not pay off because you rarely cook. The key is to calculate based on how you'll actually use it, and not to take the ad's "saves you an hour a day" as a benefit you're guaranteed to get.
extra: A supermarket farther away saves you $2 each trip, but the round trip takes an extra forty minutes. Whether it's worth going can vary from person to person. But once you factor in travel costs, time, and energy, you'll know better what you're choosing.
steps: Be clear about what you're comparing and over what time frame, such as how buying versus not buying would play out over the next year.
List the main costs of buying, learning, using, and maintaining, and also list the benefits you'd really get.
Run the key numbers once with optimistic estimates and once with conservative ones, and see whether your conclusion still holds.
caution: Money that's already spent and can't be changed shouldn't decide on its own whether you spend more later. And the time you save won't automatically turn into income, so don't count every imagined benefit as money in the bank.
exercise: Pick a tool you're thinking of buying. Besides the price, list three more costs, then write down how many times a week you'd really use it. See whether your original "great deal" needs rethinking.
brief: A cost-benefit scale over the same time frame: one side holds the coins, clock, and tools you'll need to put in later, and the other holds a basket of results and a small growing tree for the expected gains. Along a limited timeline below, two thin paths compare continuing with keeping things as they are, while a stick figure checks the baseline conditions.
